original.text:
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

prose.text: Briggs tested games alongside their writers-programmers. Testing included finding plausible player actions that a fictional world had not accounted for, not just crashes or coding errors. Romance was her own choice, not management's assignment. She wanted an adventure written from a female perspective and disliked the trivial cooking or sewing games then sold to girls. Some reviewers disliked the heroine's permitted actions and wanted a stronger fighter. Briggs regarded romance as a legitimate form, even when critics treated a woman writing for women as a limitation. Steve Meretzky encouraged her to apply as an implementer. Her application game used an abstract setting so realistic details would not expose gaps in her implementation skills. Infocom initially allowed writers considerable freedom. Briggs later remembered creative neglect and trust fondly; after Cornerstone failed and Activision acquired the company, layoffs and micromanagement changed her experience. She spent months cutting a completed Plundered Hearts to fit machines including the Commodore 64. She linked frequent player deaths to simplifying puzzles and remembered bugs that escaped testing. Management wanted another commercial hit, while her vampire and Doctor Who proposals went nowhere. Plundered Hearts sold about half Infocom's average; she eventually left amid demands without clear creative direction. Years later, players told her the game had mattered to them, despite its disappointing sales. She understood text adventures as closer to books than films, involving imagined environments and play.

Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.

Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.

cases.game_history:
>SHOOT THE PIRATE
Trembling, you fire the heavy arquebus. You hear its loud report over the
roaring wind, yet the dark figure still approaches. The gun falls from your
nerveless hands.
   "You won't kill me," he says, stepping over the weapon. "Not when I am
the only protection you have from Jean Lafond."
   Chestnut hair, tousled by the wind, frames the tanned oval of his face.
Lips curving, his eyes rake over your inadequately dressed body, the damp
chemise clinging to your legs and heaving bosom, your gleaming hair. You
are intensely aware of the strength of his hard seaworn body, of the deep
sea blue of his eyes. And then his mouth is on yours, lips parted,
demanding, and you arch into his kiss...
   He presses you against him, head bent. "But who, my dear," he whispers
into your hair, "will protect you from me?"

PLUNDERED HEARTS
Infocom interactive fiction
Copyright (c) 1987 by Infocom, Inc. All rights reserved.
PLUNDERED HEARTS is a trademark of Infocom, Inc.
Release 26 / Serial number 870730

LATE ONE SPRING NIGHT IN THE WEST INDIES...

   A crash overhead! Pirates are boarding the Lafond Deux! The first mate
hurries you into Captain Davis's cabin.
   "Good, you brought the girl," Davis smirks. "She'll keep the pirates
busy. She was only a tool of Lafond's, anyway. Let me just find that cof--"
A man on deck screams in agony and Davis starts. "Let's go." The captain
thrusts you on the bed and walks out, locking the door.
   His laugh echoes. "Best get comfortable, girl. You're likely to be there
for the rest of your life."

Cabin, on the bed
   You are in an officer's cabin, lit by the firelight glowing through a
porthole. A door is to starboard. Except for the built-in bed, the room
seems to have been emptied thoroughly, if hurriedly.

>

>> OPEN CURTAIN
You pull the cloth aside momentarily. Behind it, a large cupboard mostly
blocks the doorway.

>
>> EXAMINE CUPBOARD
You can see only the back of the large cupboard. You might be able to
squeeze past it.

>
>> EXAMINE TABLE
You have no need for that, milady.

>
>> EXAMINE BED
Someone appears to have tumbled out of it in a hurry.

>
>> WAIT
Time passes...
   You hear the large cupboard scrape, and turn to see Captain Jamison.
"Hello! I came down to give you this -- my allotment from the coffer." He
nods at the box in his arms.
   Jamison starts to pin a jewelled brooch on your clothes, but, "Devil
take it, the clasp is broken. I'll have it repaired." He folds the pretty
thing into your hand. "And I meant to reassure you that if the men suddenly
abandon ship, they are off to help me. Rodney will stay behind with you."
He drops the coffer on the floor, smiling in farewell, and walks swiftly
away.

>
recent_comments: Jamison shifts from discussing his violent intent and revenge to offering a seemingly protective, personal gesture. This sudden intimacy, coupled with his lingering gaze, creates a profound tension against the backdrop of the ship's inherent danger.

Jamison emphasizes that Lafond has bought respectability, yet this status is immediately undercut by the memory of his past actions. The assertion that he "shall never buy peace" suggests that material success cannot erase the stain of violence.

cases.game_history:
>> NORTH
Crew's Quarters
   The crew sleeps, in shifts, in this cramped space under the forecastle.
A breeze blows in on a moonbeam through a grate in the ceiling. A low
doorsill is abaft.
   This area must also serve as sickroom. Strewn about the floor are
various powders and spills of malodorous potions. In one corner, a large
blood stain indicates an amputation; in another is the smear of a leech,
dropped off a bloodletting.
   A small bottle has been dropped nearby.
   A chipped piece of mirror sits propped on a shoulder-high timber.

>
>> TAKE BOTTLE
Taken.
   "I gotta let Lafond know 'e's comin'." Crulley stands on deck above,
talking to himself, his voice floating down through a grate in the ceiling.
"First, I do in the mates aboard-ship, with this and t'other mischief," he
grunts, and you hear a snapping noise, like a taut rope being cut. "Now to
warn the boss and collect me pay. Off I go, har." He dives into the sea.

>
recent_comments: The invitation promises a formal dance at a mansion, a world of polished society. This promise stands in sharp contrast to the gloomy, damp reality of the ship's aft hold.

The tiny glow of fire creeps across the floor inside the cage of ammunition. This small, contained blaze threatens the entire store of gunpowder and shot, turning a resource of defense into a potential disaster.

cases.game_history:
>> EXAMINE WINCH
Made of an old barrel turning on a pole, the mooring winch is used to coil
in the anchor chain. A pair of metal teeth bite the links to prevent it
from dragging out; a lever is connected to the teeth. Something is written
on the lever.

>
>> READ LEVER
On the lever is written "Open Up, Close Down." You notice the lever is
pointed down.

>
>> PULL LEVER UP
The metal teeth open as you raise up the lever. The anchor, released,
splashes down into the sea, dragging its clanking chain. After a moment,
you feel the ship pull slightly against the current. You lower the lever to
prevent any more chain from spooling out.

>
>> SOUTH
Main Deck

>
>> EXAMINE BARRELS
The two open barrels contain rum and water, you can tell by the smell of
each. They are identical but for the dark stains around the mouth of the
rum barrel.
   With a heave and creak of timbers, the Helena Louise drifts a little way
back towards the island. The tide has turned.

>
recent_comments: The men move quietly under the shadows of the navigation wheel. Despite this calm, the cannons are lined up and the casks are stacked high, suggesting a latent tension beneath the moonlight.
The pirates sing low shanties while simultaneously repairing cannons and sharpening daggers. This casual rhythm of labor feels strangely at odds with the heavy, inky shadow cast by the mainmast.

The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.

Romance was her own choice, not management's assignment. She wanted an adventure written from a female perspective and disliked the trivial cooking or sewing games then sold to girls. Some reviewers disliked the heroine's permitted actions and wanted a stronger fighter. Briggs regarded romance as a legitimate form, even when critics treated a woman writing for women as a limitation. Steve Meretzky encouraged her to apply as an implementer. Her application game used an abstract setting so realistic details would not expose gaps in her implementation skills. Infocom initially allowed writers considerable freedom. Briggs later remembered creative neglect and trust fondly; after Cornerstone failed and Activision acquired the company, layoffs and micromanagement changed her experience. She spent months cutting a completed Plundered Hearts to fit machines including the Commodore 64. She linked frequent player deaths to simplifying puzzles and remembered bugs that escaped testing. Management wanted another commercial hit, while her vampire and Doctor Who proposals went nowhere. Plundered Hearts sold about half Infocom's average; she eventually left amid demands without clear creative direction. Years later, players told her the game had mattered to them, despite its disappointing sales. She understood text adventures as closer to books than films, involving imagined environments and play.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Testing fictional worlds: She tested plausible player actions that writers had not implemented, alongside ordinary software bugs.
Choosing romance: Writing romance from a heroine's perspective was her choice, not a commission from management.
Players and the heroine: Some critics wanted a heroine who could fight, and attacked the restrictions on her actions.
Becoming an author: Her abstract application game avoided realistic details that might expose gaps in implementation.
Working conditions: Creative freedom and trust gave way to layoffs and micromanagement after Cornerstone's failure.
Editing and bugs: Fitting the completed game into limited computer memory required months of cuts; some bugs remained.
Sales and next projects: Management demanded a hit but rejected her next proposals, including vampires and Doctor Who.
Readers and the medium: Low sales contrasted with players' lasting attachment; she compared text adventures to books.
END OF BACKGROUND

GAME HISTORY (oldest first, all events already seen):
>SHOOT THE PIRATE
Trembling, you fire the heavy arquebus. You hear its loud report over the
roaring wind, yet the dark figure still approaches. The gun falls from your
nerveless hands.
   "You won't kill me," he says, stepping over the weapon. "Not when I am
the only protection you have from Jean Lafond."
   Chestnut hair, tousled by the wind, frames the tanned oval of his face.
Lips curving, his eyes rake over your inadequately dressed body, the damp
chemise clinging to your legs and heaving bosom, your gleaming hair. You
are intensely aware of the strength of his hard seaworn body, of the deep
sea blue of his eyes. And then his mouth is on yours, lips parted,
demanding, and you arch into his kiss...
   He presses you against him, head bent. "But who, my dear," he whispers
into your hair, "will protect you from me?"

PLUNDERED HEARTS
Infocom interactive fiction

PLUNDERED HEARTS is a trademark of Infocom, Inc.
Release 26 / Serial number 870730

LATE ONE SPRING NIGHT IN THE WEST INDIES...

   A crash overhead! Pirates are boarding the Lafond Deux! The first mate
hurries you into Captain Davis's cabin.
   "Good, you brought the girl," Davis smirks. "She'll keep the pirates
busy. She was only a tool of Lafond's, anyway. Let me just find that cof--"
A man on deck screams in agony and Davis starts. "Let's go." The captain
thrusts you on the bed and walks out, locking the door.
   His laugh echoes. "Best get comfortable, girl. You're likely to be there
for the rest of your life."

Cabin, on the bed
   You are in an officer's cabin, lit by the firelight glowing through a
porthole. A door is to starboard. Except for the built-in bed, the room
seems to have been emptied thoroughly, if hurriedly.

>

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Briggs tested games alongside their writers-programmers. Testing included finding plausible player actions that a fictional world had not accounted for, not just crashes or coding errors. Romance was her own choice, not management's assignment. She wanted an adventure written from a female perspective and disliked the trivial cooking or sewing games then sold to girls. Some reviewers disliked the heroine's permitted actions and wanted a stronger fighter. Briggs regarded romance as a legitimate form, even when critics treated a woman writing for women as a limitation. Steve Meretzky encouraged her to apply as an implementer. Her application game used an abstract setting so realistic details would not expose gaps in her implementation skills. Infocom initially allowed writers considerable freedom. Briggs later remembered creative neglect and trust fondly; after Cornerstone failed and Activision acquired the company, layoffs and micromanagement changed her experience. She spent months cutting a completed Plundered Hearts to fit machines including the Commodore 64. She linked frequent player deaths to simplifying puzzles and remembered bugs that escaped testing. Management wanted another commercial hit, while her vampire and Doctor Who proposals went nowhere. Plundered Hearts sold about half Infocom's average; she eventually left amid demands without clear creative direction. Years later, players told her the game had mattered to them, despite its disappointing sales. She understood text adventures as closer to books than films, involving imagined environments and play.
END OF BACKGROUND

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

Testing fictional worlds:
Briggs tested games alongside their writers-programmers. Testing included finding plausible player actions that a fictional world had not accounted for, not just crashes or coding errors.

Choosing romance:
Romance was her own choice, not management's assignment. She wanted an adventure written from a female perspective and disliked the trivial cooking or sewing games then sold to girls.

Players and the heroine:
Some reviewers disliked the heroine's permitted actions and wanted a stronger fighter. Briggs regarded romance as a legitimate form, even when critics treated a woman writing for women as a limitation.

Becoming an author:
Steve Meretzky encouraged her to apply as an implementer. Her application game used an abstract setting so realistic details would not expose gaps in her implementation skills.

Working conditions:
Infocom initially allowed writers considerable freedom. Briggs later remembered creative neglect and trust fondly; after Cornerstone failed and Activision acquired the company, layoffs and micromanagement changed her experience.

Editing and bugs:
She spent months cutting a completed Plundered Hearts to fit machines including the Commodore 64. She linked frequent player deaths to simplifying puzzles and remembered bugs that escaped testing.

Sales and next projects:
Management wanted another commercial hit, while her vampire and Doctor Who proposals went nowhere. Plundered Hearts sold about half Infocom's average; she eventually left amid demands without clear creative direction.

Readers and the medium:
Years later, players told her the game had mattered to them, despite its disappointing sales. She understood text adventures as closer to books than films, involving imagined environments and play.

>SHOOT THE PIRATE
Trembling, you fire the heavy arquebus. You hear its loud report over the
roaring wind, yet the dark figure still approaches. The gun falls from your
nerveless hands.
   "You won't kill me," he says, stepping over the weapon. "Not when I am
the only protection you have from Jean Lafond."
   Chestnut hair, tousled by the wind, frames the tanned oval of his face.
Lips curving, his eyes rake over your inadequately dressed body, the damp
chemise clinging to your legs and heaving bosom, your gleaming hair. You
are intensely aware of the strength of his hard seaworn body, of the deep
sea blue of his eyes. And then his mouth is on yours, lips parted,
demanding, and you arch into his kiss...
   He presses you against him, head bent. "But who, my dear," he whispers
into your hair, "will protect you from me?"

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Testing fictional worlds:
Briggs tested games alongside their writers-programmers. Testing included finding plausible player actions that a fictional world had not accounted for, not just crashes or coding errors.

Choosing romance:
Romance was her own choice, not management's assignment. She wanted an adventure written from a female perspective and disliked the trivial cooking or sewing games then sold to girls.

Players and the heroine:
Some reviewers disliked the heroine's permitted actions and wanted a stronger fighter. Briggs regarded romance as a legitimate form, even when critics treated a woman writing for women as a limitation.

Becoming an author:
Steve Meretzky encouraged her to apply as an implementer. Her application game used an abstract setting so realistic details would not expose gaps in her implementation skills.

Working conditions:
Infocom initially allowed writers considerable freedom. Briggs later remembered creative neglect and trust fondly; after Cornerstone failed and Activision acquired the company, layoffs and micromanagement changed her experience.

Editing and bugs:
She spent months cutting a completed Plundered Hearts to fit machines including the Commodore 64. She linked frequent player deaths to simplifying puzzles and remembered bugs that escaped testing.

Sales and next projects:
Management wanted another commercial hit, while her vampire and Doctor Who proposals went nowhere. Plundered Hearts sold about half Infocom's average; she eventually left amid demands without clear creative direction.

Readers and the medium:
Years later, players told her the game had mattered to them, despite its disappointing sales. She understood text adventures as closer to books than films, involving imagined environments and play.
END OF BACKGROUND

2. Jamison emphasizes that Lafond has bought respectability, yet this status is immediately undercut by the memory of his past actions. The assertion that he "shall never buy peace" suggests that material success cannot erase the stain of violence.

OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. OPTIONAL BACKGROUND: AMY BRIGGS'S TESTIMONY
Amy Briggs recounts her experience at Infocom as a mixture of chance, creative intensity, and gradual disillusionment. She entered the company almost accidentally in the early 1980s, after breaking up with a boyfriend and impulsively deciding to move to Massachusetts. Discovering a job ad for game testers at Infocom, she applied, was quickly hired, and found herself inside a company that felt unlike any workplace she had known. At the time, she had little sense of how unusual Infocom was, as it was her first job out of college.
Briggs began as a tester, part of a group closely connected to the implementers (“Imps”), the writers-programmers responsible for Infocom’s games. Testing was not merely about finding crashes or bugs, but about identifying where a fictional world broke down—where player expectations exceeded what the game could reasonably implement. This role gave her an unusually deep understanding of how text adventures were built, from early, broken alpha versions to finished works. That proximity made the transition from tester to implementer feel natural rather than aspirational.
Her move into game creation came at a precarious moment in Infocom’s history. The company was expanding, relocating to a sleek new office, and betting heavily on Cornerstone, a business software product meant to transform Infocom into a more “serious” company. Briggs recalls being swept up in the excitement of this shift, even though it ultimately proved disastrous. As Cornerstone failed and Infocom was acquired by Activision, layoffs followed and the internal atmosphere changed. The free, lightly managed creative culture that had allowed the games group to flourish began to erode under pressure and fear.
Encouraged by Steve Meretzky, Briggs decided to apply for an implementer position. She was told bluntly that opportunities were rare and that if she wanted the job, she had to act immediately. Her test game was deliberately strange and abstract, avoiding realistic settings that might expose weaknesses in her implementation skills. She was hired, becoming one of the few women to design an Infocom game. Her first project was Plundered Hearts, a romantic, swashbuckling adventure written from a female perspective.
Briggs emphasizes that Plundered Hearts was not imposed on her by management. Writing romance aligned with her own interests and her long-standing desire to explore that genre. At the time, “games for girls” were often condescending or trivial, and she saw romance as a legitimate narrative form rather than a marketing gimmick. Still, the game’s positioning as “a woman writing for women” became central to its reception, sometimes in ways she found frustrating. Some critics accused the game of being anti-feminist because it constrained the protagonist’s actions, while others dismissed it for not conforming to expectations of empowerment.
From a technical perspective, Plundered Hearts was ambitious and difficult. Briggs completed it early, then spent months cutting content to fit the memory constraints of platforms like the Commodore 64. Space limitations shaped design decisions, including frequent player deaths, which served as a crude but effective way to simplify puzzle design. She also recalls lingering embarrassment over bugs that slipped into the final release, highlighting how even experienced testing could miss obvious player actions.
Commercially, the game underperformed by Infocom’s standards, selling roughly half of what an average title sold at the time. Internally, this was treated as a disappointment, though Briggs stresses that nearly every game not matching Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy was judged similarly. Years later, however, she was surprised and moved to discover that Plundered Hearts had left a lasting impression on players, particularly those who encountered it indirectly through siblings. What she had experienced as a failed experiment was remembered by others as meaningful and formative.
After Plundered Hearts, Briggs struggled to find alignment with management about future projects. She proposed ideas ranging from vampire fiction inspired by Anne Rice to Doctor Who, but none gained traction. Increasingly, Infocom’s leadership demanded guaranteed commercial success without offering clear creative direction. This contradiction, combined with the broader panic following Cornerstone’s collapse, made continued work untenable. She ultimately left Infocom, convinced that what had made the company great—creative neglect and trust—had been replaced by micromanagement and fear.
Looking back, Briggs describes Infocom as a brief “Camelot”: a rare moment when individual vision, technical constraint, and collaborative support aligned. She remains skeptical that such conditions can easily be recreated, particularly in an industry now dominated by large teams, heavy budgets, and cinematic expectations. For her, text adventures were closer to books than films, and Infocom’s legacy lies in that unique blend of literature and play.
END OF BACKGROUND
